Stiff-man Syndrome: Case Report 
Walter F. Kuhn, MD, Peter J. Light, MD, 
Sharon C. Kuhn, MD 
I ABSTRACT 
Stiff-man syndrome is a rare neurologic disorder characterized by 
progressive, fluctuating muscle rigidity with painful muscle contrac- 
tions affecting predominantly the back and proximal extremities. In 
the ED, the diagnosis can be easily overlooked and misdiagnosed as 
acute or chronic low back pain and muscle spasm. This syndrome is 
often associated with diabetes, autoimmune diseases, and cancer. 
This report describes an illustrative case of a 39-year-old woman who 
presented to the ED with a two-year history of right leg spasms and 
low back pain that had become so severe in the preceding two days 
that she was unable to ambulate. Clues to the patient’s proper di- 
agnosis coincide with the diagnostic criteria for stiff-man syndrome: 
the presence of a slowly progressive stiffness of the axial muscles and 
proximal limb muscles, making ambulation difficult; hyperlordosis of 
the lumbar spine; episodic spasms precipitated by jarring or sudden 
movement; a normal intellectual, sensory, and motor examination 
when not in spasm; and a marked amelioration of symptoms with the 
IV administration of diazepam. High-dose oral diazepam is the main- 
tenance drug of choice.

I The stiff-man syndrome is a rare neurologic disease characterized 
by episodes of progressive, rigid stiffness of the axial and limb mus- 
culature with superimposed painful muscle spasms. The syndrome is 
not well known by emergency physicians (EPs). Because of its non- 
specific presentation, it may be overlooked or erroneously diagnosed 
as a psychiatric disorder, drug-seeking behavior, opisthotonic extra- 
pyramidal reaction to drugs, tetanus, or other musculoskeletal back 
and limb pain. The syndrome is frequently associated with diabetes, 
autoimmune diseases, and cancer. Stiff-man syndrome is usually not 
life-threatening but it can cause significant long-term morbidity. The 
exact mechanism of the disorder is not fully understood but it is 
believed to have an autoimmune basis. Treatment has been successful 
with high doses of benzodiazepines. This case report describes a 
patient who presented to the ED with stiff-man syndrome and dis- 
cusses the diagnosis, etiology, immunology, and management of this 
rare disease. 
I CASEREPORT 
History 
A 39-year-old black woman who had back pain was carried into 
the ED by two relatives. She related that she had had severe, inter-

mittent back spasms over the preceding week. Two days earlier, she 
had seen an orthopedist who had treated her with diazepam, 5 mg 
bid, and chlorzoxazone, 500 mg qid. He had referred her to a neu-

rologist the following day, but upon arrival at the neu- 
rologist’s office, the woman driving the patient had been 
unable to get the patient out of the car due to the 
severity of her back spasms. 
The patient reported similar but less intense low 
back pains and severe right leg spasms over the pre- 
ceding year. Review of her medical record showed a 
history of low back pain with spasms and right lower- 
extremity spasms for about three years. Magnetic res- 
onance imaging of the cervical spine three years pre- 
viously had been unremarkable, and MRI of the lum- 
bosacral spine one year earlier had been inconclusive. 
Electromyography (EMG) performed at that time had 
been inconclusive. 
The patient’s review of systems was significant for 
occasional vomiting when she attempted to take med- 
ications. The patient denied any recent travel or history 
of skin lesions or wounds, fever, chills, night sweats, or 
incontinence. Her past medical history was significant 
for a vitamin B12 deficiency and atrophic gastritis for 
which she received monthly B12 injections. There was 
no history of a psychiatric disorder. Her only other 
medications were those prescribed in the three days 
prior, which included the diazepam and chlorzoxazone 
mentioned above and zolpidem tartrate, 10 mg qh. Her 
tetanus immunization was not current. 
Physical Examination 
On physical examination the patient was alert, ori- 
ented, and anxious, with unremarkable vital signs, ex- 
cept tachycardia during spasms. She had intermittent 
spasms of the trunk with arching posture, lasting 2 to 
5 minutes. These episodes of opisthotonos seemed trig- 
gered by external stimuli (e.g., by opening the door, 
speaking, and tactile stimuli, but not by loud noises). 
Between episodes, the patient was alert and comfort- 
able, and her neurologic examination was unremarka- 
ble. Her cranial nerves were intact and symmetrical; 
her reflexes were +2 and equal bilaterally; there were 
normal tone and strength in all extremities, and sen- 
sation was normal for pain and light touch. Her straight 
leg test was negative bilaterally. 
The patient experienced moderate to severe para- 
spinal spasm, with a mild-moderate hyperlordosis dur- 
ing spasms. During the spasms the patient became op- 
isthotonic and so rigid that continued examination was 
impossible. However, she remained alert and cried out 
in pain. Her abdominal musculature was board-like to 
palpation, with normal bowel sounds. Initial laboratory 
data showed a mild anemia and a serum bicarbonate of 
15 mmoVL, presumed secondary to lactic acid from the 
severe muscle contractions. Electrolytes, WBCs, uri- 
nalysis, creatine kinase, and calcium were within nor- 
mal limits. 
Clinical Course 
The patient was given diazepam, 5 mg IV, with con- 
trol of symptoms for approximately 30 minutes. She 
was admitted to the neurology service with the working 
diagnosis of stiff-man syndrome. Needle EMG showed 
increased volitional activity and poor relaxation, par- 
ticularly in the right tibialis anterior and lumbosacral 
paraspinal muscles in association with severe spasm. A 
lumbar puncture for anti-glutamic acid decarboxylase 
(anti-GAD) antibodies was done. (Several months after 
discharge, a positive result was obtained.) A placebo 
saline challenge test showed no relief of spasm. The 
patient was treated with increasing doses of diazepam

and her symptoms were finally controlled on a 10-mg 
qid dose. She was discharged after four days in the 
hospital with the diagnosis of probable stiff-man syn- 
drome. 
I DISCUSSION 
One of the key features in the presentation of this pa- 
tient was the chronic, recurrent nature of her com- 
plaints, which made the diagnoses of drug reaction, 
envenomation, or tetanus much less likely. The seventy 
of her muscle spasm in contrast with an otherwise nor- 
mal neurologic examination provided another diagnos- 
tic clue. It is of note that this patient had been seen on 
several prior occasions and had undergone multiple di- 
agnostic tests before this visit without being properly 
diagnosed. 
Stiff-man syndrome was first described by Moersch 
and Woltman’ in 1956, in a series of 14 cases at the 
Mayo Clinic. Over the last 38 years, 100 patients have 
been described with this disorder, primarily in the neu- 
rology literature. The disease is characterized by a pe- 
riodic rigid stiffness of the axial and limb musculature 
with superimposed painful spasms that are precipitated 
by movement, startling, or emotional stimuli. Except 
for the absence of trismus and its chronic, progressive 
nature, the stiff-man syndrome acutely resembles tet- 
anus. In 1967 Gordon et aL2 proposed diagnostic cri- 
teria. Lorish et aL3 updated the diagnostic criteria after 
reviewing all published accounts of the disease. The 
updated diagnostic criteria for stiff-man syndrome4 are 
represented by the first seven items in Table 1. 
The initial symptoms of stiff-man syndrome are in- 
sidious and typically mild, “including intermittent tight- 
ness and rigidity usually in the lower back but often 
also in the neck or proximal portion of the limbs.”4 
“With time, this becomes more persistent and is punc- 
tuated by spasms of increased muscle stiffness and 
ngidity’l4 lasting up to several minutes, precipitated by 
sudden movement, noises, touch, or emotional upset. 
These spasms may be sufficiently painful to cause pro- 
fuse sweating and a rise in the blood pressure for many

patients. Between spasms, there may be persistent ri- 
gidity of the back, abdomen, and limbs, making am- 
bulation difficult, although the distal musculature and 
facial musculature are usually spared. Symptoms may 
progress over months to years. The spinal defoimity 
emphasized by Lorish et aL3 may be helpful in differ- 
entiating stiff-man syndrome from other causes of mus- 
cle rigidity or stiffness. The deformity can progress to 
a fixed lumbar hyperlordosis and a “permanent ‘shrug’ 
of the shoulders with the neck drawn down into the 
shoulder girdle.”4 In long-standing cases, there may be 
hypertrophy of the paraspinal musculature. 
Otherwise the physical examination is normal, ex- 
cept that deep tendon reflexes may be symmetrically in- 
creased. The affected muscles reveal a tight, board-like 
quality, most often in the paravertebral and abdominal 
areas. No laboratory test is diagnostic of stiff-man syn- 
drome. Neurophysiologic studies have demonstrated the 
presence of continuous discharge of motor-unit poten- 
tials resembling a normal voluntary contraction with 
superimposed generalized paroxysmal muscle contrac- 
tions comprised of simultaneous contraction of agonistic 
and antagonistic mu~cles.~ These motor-unit discharges 
may be extinguished with IV diazepam, myoneural block, 
motor nerve block, or general anesthesia. The EEG is 
normal, but sleep studies often show long latencies be- 
tween wakefulness and stage 1 sleep due to muscle spasm. 
In stage 2, muscle spasms disappear and sleep proceeds 
normally. Table 1 lists the diagnostic features of stiff- 
man syndr~me.~ 
Of the patients described in the literature, the male- 
to-female ratio is approximately 3:2.6 Ages range from 
8 to 76 years, with an average of just over 40 years. 
About 30% have diabetes, nearly 40% are reported to 
have some form of autoimmune disorder, and about 
5% are reported to have a seizure di~rder.~ Autoim- 
mune hsorders that have been described with stiff-man 
syndrome include “Hashimoto’s thyroiditis, Graves’ 
disease, myasthenia gravis, autoimmune adrenal fail- 
ure, ovarian failure, vitiligo, and pernicious anemia.” 
There have been a few reports of stiff-man syndrome 
among patients who had breast and colon cancers, sug- 
gesting the possibility of a paraneoplastic form of the 
The etiology of stiff-man syndrome is unknown; 
however, it responds dramatically to the benzodiaze- 
pines, which are gamma-aminobutyric acid (GABA) 
agonists. There is good evidence that benzodiazepines 
potentiate GABA-receptor activity. This has led to the 
suggestion that stiff-man syndrome is a disorder of the 
central GABA-receptor pathways.6 In 1988, Solimena 
and De CamilliR described an autoantibody, in a type 
1 diabetic patient, that bound to GAD. Because GAD 
is the rate-limiting enzyme in the production of GABA 
in neurons, an antibody directed against GAD was con-

sistent with the hypothesis of GABA-receptor dys- 
function in stiff-man syndrome. Several patients who 
had stiff-man syndrome have been tested and found to 
have anti-GAD antibodies, although other patients have 
not shown this antibody. 
Diazepam remains the treatment of choice since being 
introduced by Howard9 in 1963. It markedly diminishes 
continuous motor activity but does not alter the natural 
history of the disease. Diazepam must be used in doses 
from 40 to 300 mg per day, to be effective. Baclofen 
has been tried with variable ~uccess.~ Valproate, which 
is believed to facilitate GABA receptors, clonidine, and 
clonazepam also have been used with varied success. lo 
There have been case reports suggesting that plasma- 
pheresis may be helpful for patients who have high 
serum titers of antibodies with GAD-like immunoreac- 
tivity.*l Other authors have shown no improvement. 
Likewise, there have been varied reports of the effec- 
tiveness of prednisoneI2 and immunosuppression ther- 
apy. Nonsteroidal therapy has not been examined. 
I CONCLUSION 
Stiff-man syndrome is a rare disorder manifesting as 
prominent, progressive, painful muscle contractions of 
the axial musculature. Because it is rare, a high index 
of suspicion must be maintained by EPs. The diagnosis 
is primarily made clinically. Hyperlordosis of the back, 
along with periodic, painful muscle contractions lasting 
several minutes and exacerbated by movement, emo- 
tional, or tactile stimuli, should alert the clinician to the 
possible diagnosis. There may be concurrent diabetes, 
autoimmune syndromes, or cancer. Anti-GAD anti- 
bodies may be present but offer no help to the clinician 
in the acute setting because they are not universally 
present and are available only in a few reference lab- 
oratories. The mainstay of treatment remains high doses 
of diazepam, which offer significant relief from the mus- 
cle contractions. Other therapies are under investiga- 
tion and have met with varied success.
